1.note: See how you translated this phrase in 1:12.

2.q: וְ⁠שֵׁ֥ם מִשְׁנֵ֖⁠הוּ אֲבִיָּ֑ה שֹׁפְטִ֖ים בִּ⁠בְאֵ֥ר שָֽׁבַע
2.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the name of his second son was Abijah, and they both served as judges in Beersheba]
If your language does not use ordinal numbers, you can use a cardinal number here or an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [Samuel’s son number two]

3.note: The author is speaking as if **ways** were paths that Samuel’s sons could walk on. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But his sons did not live the way he had lived]

The author is speaking as if Samuel’s sons were walking on a path but **turned** off it in order to go in the direction where **dishonest gain** was. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [instead, they tried to get money dishonestly]
The author is not referring to a specific **bribe**. He means bribes in general. It may be more natural in your language to express this meaning by using a plural form as in the UST.

The author is speaking as if **justice** were something that Samuel’s sons could have caused to leave a path that it was walking on. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they did not judge cases fairly]

5.note: See how you translated this term in 2:31.
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:3. Alternate translation: [and your sons do not live the way you have lived]

By **us**, the Israelite elders mean themselves but perhaps not Samuel, since they are speaking of what they want the situation to be for themselves after he dies. So it may be appropriate to use the exclusive form of “us” in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

6.note: See the discussion in the Introduction to 1 Samuel of this use of the expression “in the eyes of.” The author is using this common expression of his culture to refer to the judgment or opinion of Samuel. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Samuel considered this request to be wrong]

7.note: See the discussion of the term “listen” in the Introduction to 1 Samuel, and see how you translated the similar expression in 2:25. Alternate translation: [Obey the voice of the people]

The author is using the term **voice** to represent what the people asked for by using their collective voice. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Do what the people have asked for]
Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but a further observation. Alternate translation: [In fact]

8.note: The author is using the term **day** in this phrase to represent a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the time]

9.note: See how you translated the expression “And now” in 6:7. Alternate translation: [So this is what I want you to do]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:7. Alternate translation: [do what they are asking for]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **warn** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [you must warn them very strongly]

10.note: The author is using the term **words** to represent what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everything that Yahweh had told him]

11.note: The words **you** and **your** are plural here and through verse 18 because Samuel is addressing the Israelite elders, so use plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Samuel is not referring to a specific **chariot**. He means chariots in general. It may be more natural in your language to express this meaning by using a plural form. Alternate translation: [to drive his chariots]

This was a symbolic action that showed the king’s power and authority by having servants run ahead of his chariot to clear the way and announce his coming. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action. Alternate translation: [and they will run ahead of his chariot to show everyone how important he is]
See the discussion of the phrase “to the face” in the Introduction to 1 Samuel, and see how you translated the phrase in 1:12. Alternate translation: [ahead of his chariot]

12.q: וְ⁠לַ⁠חֲרֹ֤שׁ חֲרִישׁ⁠וֹ֙ וְ⁠לִ⁠קְצֹ֣ר קְצִיר֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠לַ⁠עֲשׂ֥וֹת כְּלֵֽי־מִלְחַמְתּ֖⁠וֹ וּ⁠כְלֵ֥י רִכְבּֽ⁠וֹ
12.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he will force some of them to plow his fields and harvest his crops, and he will force others to make weapons for his army and equipment for his chariots]

For emphasis, Samuel is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of showing the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and to do all his plowing and all his harvesting]
Samuel is not referring to a specific **chariot**. He means chariots in general. It may be more natural in your language to express this meaning by using a plural form as in the UST.

13.note: A **perfumer** is someone who makes substances such as oils that give off pleasant smells. If your readers would not be familiar with what a perfumer is, in your translation you could use the name of a similar occupation that your readers would recognize, or you could use a general expression. Alternate translation: [for people who make sweet-smelling oils]

14.q: וְ⁠אֶת־שְׂ֠דֽוֹתֵי⁠כֶם וְ⁠אֶת־כַּרְמֵי⁠כֶ֧ם וְ⁠זֵיתֵי⁠כֶ֛ם הַ⁠טּוֹבִ֖ים יִקָּ֑ח וְ⁠נָתַ֖ן לַ⁠עֲבָדָֽי⁠ו
14.note: It may be more natural in your language to put the word **best**, which provides information about what kind of fields, vineyards, and olive trees the king will take, at the start of the verse with the information that he will take them. Alternate translation: [And he will take your best fields and vineyards and olive trees and give them to his servants]

16.q: וְ⁠אֶת־עַבְדֵי⁠כֶם֩ וְֽ⁠אֶת־שִׁפְח֨וֹתֵי⁠כֶ֜ם וְ⁠אֶת־בַּחוּרֵי⁠כֶ֧ם הַ⁠טּוֹבִ֛ים וְ⁠אֶת־חֲמוֹרֵי⁠כֶ֖ם יִקָּ֑ח וְ⁠עָשָׂ֖ה לִ⁠מְלַאכְתּֽ⁠וֹ
16.note: It may be more natural in your language to put the word **best**, which provides information about what kind of servants, young men, and donkeys the king will take, at the start of the verse with the information that he will take them. Alternate translation: [And he will take your best male servants and female servants and young men and donkeys and use them for his work]

17.note: Samuel is speaking as if the Israelites would literally become slaves to the king. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and in the end, it will be as if you are his slaves]

18.note: Samuel is using the term **day** to represent a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [at that time … at that time]

Samuel is using the term **face** to represent the presence of the king, which, as he has described, will be highly intrusive and oppressive. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for relief from the oppression of your king]

See the discussion of the term “answer” in the Introduction to 1 Samuel, and see how you translated the similar expression “listen to” in 8:7. Alternate translation: [but Yahweh will not do what you ask]

19.note: The author is using the term **voice** to represent what Samuel said by using his voice. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to what Samuel told them]

20.note: The author is using the term **face** to represent the front of the army in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and go out ahead of us and fight our battles] or [and lead us into battle]

The elders are speaking of one person who would **fight** their **battles**, the king, to represent the whole army that would do this. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and go out ahead of our army as it fights its battles]

21.note: The author is using the term **words** to represent what the people said by using words. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everything that the people had said]

The author is using the term **ears** to represent hearing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for Yahweh to hear]

22.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 8:7. Alternate translation: [Do what they are asking for]

The author assumes that his readers will know that by **the men of Israel**, he means the elders who had come to speak with Samuel. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the elders of Israel]

22.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר שְׁמוּאֵל֙ אֶל־אַנְשֵׁ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל לְכ֖וּ אִ֥ישׁ לְ⁠עִירֽ⁠וֹ
22.note: It may be more natural in your language to have an indirect quotation here. Alternate translation: [And Samuel told the men of Israel to return to their cities]

The author assumes that his readers will know that Samuel is dismissing the elders because he has agreed to do what they are asking. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [You can all go home now, because I will do what you are asking]
The implied “you” in the imperative **Go** is plural because Samuel is addressing the group of elders, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Samuel is not referring to a specific **man**. He means all of the men he is addressing. It may be more natural in your language to express this meaning by using a plural form. Alternate translation: [all of to your own cities]
